title: The US Military Can’t Function Without China
gist: Modern U.S. weapons systems from the F-35 to Tomahawk missiles depend on rare earth elements that China dominates, controlling roughly 70 percent of global mining and over 90 percent of processing, and per USGS data holding at least one monopoly (mining, refining, or processing) in each of the 30 critical minerals in which it leads global production.

themes.theme: Rare earth intensity of modern weapons

insights.claim: According to the U.S. Department of Defense, an F-35 fighter jet requires more than 400 kilograms of rare earth elements to build.
insights.speaker: Justin Fendos
insights.so_what: Quantifies the direct rare-earth exposure embedded in a flagship U.S. weapons platform, a concrete figure for modeling supply-chain risk to F-35 production rates.
insights.quote: According to the U.S. Department of Defense, an F-35 fighter requires more than 400 kilograms of rare earths to build
insights.locator: According to the U.S. Department of Defense

insights.claim: A U.S. Navy destroyer or submarine requires anywhere from two to five metric tons of rare earth elements to build, respectively.
insights.speaker: Justin Fendos
insights.so_what: Naval shipbuilding carries an even larger per-unit rare-earth burden than aircraft, making U.S. fleet expansion plans directly hostage to rare-earth supply availability.
insights.quote: a destroyer and submarine, respectively, can require anywhere from two to five metric tons

insights.claim: Rare earths are also essential components in Tomahawk missiles, Predator drones, and the missiles and bombs that have been used in Iran over the last few months.
insights.speaker: Justin Fendos
insights.so_what: Extends rare-earth dependency beyond big-ticket platforms to the missiles and munitions actually being expended in current U.S. military operations, meaning any supply disruption has near-term operational consequences, not just long-term procurement ones.
insights.quote: Rare earths also appear in Tomahawk missiles, Predator drones, and the many missiles and bombs that have been used in Iran over the last few months.
insights.locator: Rare earths also appear in Tomahawk

themes.theme: China's chokehold on the rare earth supply chain

insights.claim: China accounts for roughly 70 percent of all global rare earth mining and more than 90 percent of all global rare earth processing, dominating entire categories of critical materials needed to make semiconductors, avionics, batteries, and munitions.
insights.speaker: Justin Fendos
insights.so_what: China's near-total control of rare-earth processing, not just mining, is the structural chokepoint — any diversification strategy must target processing capacity, not just alternative mine sites.
insights.quote: China accounts for roughly 70 percent of all rare earth mining and more than 90 percent of all rare earth processing, dominating entire categories of critical materials needed to make semiconductors, avionics, batteries, and things that go boom.
insights.locator: The problem for the U.S. military

insights.claim: According to the U.S. Geological Survey, China leads global production in 30 of 44 critical minerals while maintaining, in each of those 30 minerals, at least one monopoly in mining, refining, or processing.
insights.speaker: Justin Fendos
insights.so_what: Quantifies the breadth of China's critical-minerals dominance well beyond rare earths alone, underscoring the scale of the diversification challenge facing U.S. defense and tech supply chains.
insights.quote: According to the U.S. Geological Survey, China leads global production in 30 of 44 critical minerals while maintaining, in each of those 30 minerals, at least one monopoly in mining, refining, or processing.
insights.locator: According to the U.S. Geological Survey

insights.claim: The U.S. military's ability to produce modern weapons systems is structurally dependent on rare earth and critical mineral supply chains that China dominates in mining, processing, or refining.
insights.speaker: Justin Fendos
insights.so_what: Frames Chinese critical-minerals dominance as a direct strategic vulnerability for U.S. defense production, a central variable for assessing both U.S. military readiness risk and the investment case for non-Chinese rare-earth mining and processing capacity.
insights.locator: The problem for the U.S. military
